title: Anaphylaxis: age-banded IM adrenaline and escalation
blurb: Recognise anaphylaxis in a child, give the right IM adrenaline dose for age, repeat it at 5 minutes, and escalate refractory reactions using RCUK guidance.
question: Toby, 4, develops stridor, wheeze and widespread hives 10 minutes after eating a cashew at a children's day unit. What dose of IM adrenaline should the nurse give?

teach.body: Anaphylaxis is a severe, potentially life-threatening systemic allergic reaction. RCUK recognises it by sudden onset and rapid progression, plus Airway and/or Breathing and/or Circulation problems, usually with skin or mucosal changes such as hives or swelling. Skin changes are absent in up to 20% of cases. Plain English: a fast-moving reaction that affects breathing or circulation is anaphylaxis until proved otherwise, and IM adrenaline is the first treatment.

head: System
Look for
rows: Swelling of throat or tongue, hoarse voice, stridor
Increased work of breathing, wheeze, tiring, low SpO2
Signs of shock, low BP, dizziness, decreased consciousness
teach.caption: Skin or mucosal changes alone (hives, flushing) without A, B or C problems are not anaphylaxis. Gastrointestinal symptoms alone also do not meet the definition.

head: Age
Dose
Volume
teach.caption: Inject into the anterolateral thigh. If in doubt, give IM adrenaline: a single dose poses minimal risk.

steps.label: Position + oxygen
steps.sub: Lie flat or semi-recumbent; high-flow O2

steps.label: Still A, B, C problems at 5 min
steps.sub: Repeat IM adrenaline; IV fluid bolus 10 mL/kg

teach.caption: Refractory anaphylaxis: no improvement in breathing or circulation despite 2 doses of IM adrenaline. Seek expert help early for an IV adrenaline infusion.

teach.body: Sudden changes in posture can be fatal: a child must not stand, walk or sit up suddenly during a reaction. A child with airway or breathing problems may prefer to sit semi-recumbent. A child with low blood pressure should lie flat, with or without legs raised. A child who is unconscious but breathing normally goes in the recovery position.

teach.h: What is (and is not) first line
columns: Not for initial A, B, C
teach.caption: Fluids: give a 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus in a child if A, B or C problems persist, and early if there is shock.

teach.text: Watch the decimal point. IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL (1 in 1,000) contains 1,000 micrograms per mL, so 0.15 mL gives 150 micrograms. Drawing up 1.5 mL would give 1,500 micrograms: a ten-fold overdose.

teach.h: Scenario: Ruby, 5 months, on the ward
teach.body: Ruby develops facial swelling, a hoarse cry and pallor shortly after her first taste of egg. Nurse Leah recognises an airway problem with circulatory signs. She calls for help, lays Ruby flat, and gives IM adrenaline 100 to 150 micrograms (0.1 to 0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL) into the anterolateral thigh. She starts oxygen and monitoring, and prepares a second dose for 5 minutes if Ruby has not improved.

head: Situation
Observe
rows: Good response to 1 early dose, resolved, has AAIs and supervision
2 doses of IM adrenaline, or previous biphasic reaction
Over 2 doses, severe asthma or late presentation
teach.caption: Biphasic reactions occur in around 5% of cases. Before discharge: allergy clinic referral, adrenaline auto-injector training and an emergency action plan.

items: Anaphylaxis = sudden onset plus Airway, Breathing or Circulation problems.
IM adrenaline 1 mg/mL: over 12 = 500 mcg; 6–12 = 300 mcg; 6 months–6 years = 150 mcg; under 6 months = 100–150 mcg.
Repeat after 5 minutes if A, B or C problems persist; give a 10 mL/kg fluid bolus.
Refractory after 2 IM doses: expert help for IV adrenaline infusion.
Antihistamines are third line; steroids are not routine.

summary: You can now recognise anaphylaxis by its A, B and C problems, choose the correct IM adrenaline dose and volume for age, and repeat treatment at 5 minutes. You can also position the child safely, escalate refractory anaphylaxis and plan safe discharge.

A.q: Toby, 4, develops stridor, wheeze and widespread hives 10 minutes after eating a cashew. What dose of IM adrenaline should the nurse give?
A.why: For children aged 6 months to 6 years, the RCUK IM adrenaline dose is 150 micrograms (0.15 mL of 1 mg/mL).

whyNot.0: 300 micrograms is the dose for children aged 6 to 12 years.
whyNot.1: 500 micrograms is the dose for over-12s.
whyNot.2: 100 micrograms is the lower end of the under-6-months range.

A.q: Sami, 9, has anaphylaxis after a bee sting. Which dose and route is correct?
A.why: Children aged 6 to 12 years receive 300 micrograms (0.3 mL of 1 mg/mL) IM into the anterolateral thigh.

whyNot.1: The anterolateral thigh is the recommended site, not the deltoid.
whyNot.3: Adrenaline for anaphylaxis is given IM, not subcutaneously.

A.q: Five minutes after IM adrenaline for anaphylaxis, Leo, 8, remains wheezy with a respiratory rate of 34. What should happen next?
A.why: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if Airway, Breathing or Circulation problems persist.

whyNot.0: Antihistamines are third line and do not treat breathing problems in anaphylaxis.
whyNot.1: Corticosteroids are no longer advised for routine emergency treatment.
whyNot.3: Waiting delays a repeat dose that is due at 5 minutes.

B.q: Maya, 14, has reached puberty and has anaphylaxis with wheeze and a blood pressure of 78/40. What IM adrenaline dose is correct?
B.why: Over 12 years the dose is 500 micrograms (0.5 mL of 1 mg/mL); 300 micrograms is reserved for small or prepubertal children over 12.

whyNot.0: 150 micrograms is the 6 months to 6 years dose.
whyNot.2: 300 micrograms is for 6 to 12-year-olds, or small or prepubertal over-12s.
whyNot.3: 1 mg IM is double the maximum IM dose for this age.

B.q: Amira, 10, has anaphylaxis with hypotension and has received IM adrenaline. How should she be positioned?
options: Lying flat, legs raised if possible
Sitting upright in a supportive chair
B.why: RCUK: lying flat, with or without leg elevation, helps a patient with low blood pressure. Sudden sitting or standing can be fatal.

whyNot.1: Sitting upright reduces venous return in a hypotensive child.
whyNot.2: Standing during a reaction has been linked to fatal collapse.
whyNot.3: Prone positioning hinders airway and circulation assessment.

B.q: Ethan, 11, has anaphylaxis. Despite two correctly given IM adrenaline doses 5 minutes apart, he remains hypotensive and wheezy. What is this, and what is needed?
options: A biphasic reaction; observe for 12 hours
Refractory; expert help for IV adrenaline
A failed injection; give a third IM dose and wait
B.why: Anaphylaxis that does not improve after 2 appropriate IM doses is refractory. RCUK advises early expert help and an IV adrenaline infusion, with fluids.

whyNot.0: A biphasic reaction recurs after resolution; Ethan has not improved at all.
whyNot.2: IM doses can continue every 5 minutes, but refractory anaphylaxis needs expert help for IV adrenaline.
whyNot.3: Salbutamol may help wheeze but does not treat refractory anaphylaxis with shock.

C.q: Olivia, 7, weighs 24 kg. After a second IM adrenaline dose her blood pressure is still low. What IV fluid bolus is appropriate?
C.why: RCUK advises a 10 mL/kg crystalloid bolus in a child: 10 x 24 = 240 mL.

whyNot.1: 120 mL is 5 mL/kg, half the recommended bolus.
whyNot.2: 500 mL is an adult bolus volume.

C.q: Josh, 6, had anaphylaxis to peanut. He responded within 5 minutes to one dose of IM adrenaline given 10 minutes after onset. His symptoms have fully resolved, he has unused auto-injectors he is trained to use, and his parents are with him. What observation period can be considered?
C.why: RCUK 2021: fast-track discharge after 2 hours can be considered with a good response to a single early dose, complete resolution, trained auto-injector user and adequate supervision.

whyNot.0: 24 hours is not part of the RCUK risk-stratified approach.
whyNot.1: 12 hours is for severe reactions needing more than 2 doses, severe asthma or late presentation.
whyNot.3: 6 hours is advised after 2 doses or a previous biphasic reaction.

C.q: Zain, 3, has widespread hives and lip swelling after eating egg. His breathing, voice and circulation are normal. What is the most appropriate action?
C.why: Skin and mucosal changes without A, B or C problems are not anaphylaxis. A non-sedating oral antihistamine and close observation for progression are appropriate.

whyNot.0: IM adrenaline is for Airway, Breathing or Circulation problems, which he does not have.
whyNot.1: Steroids are not part of routine emergency allergy treatment.
whyNot.3: A fluid bolus treats circulatory compromise, which he does not have.

reteach.title: A, B or C plus adrenaline
reteach.question: What turns an allergic reaction into anaphylaxis, and what is the one drug that matters first?

blocks.body: Hives on their own are an allergic reaction. Add an Airway problem (stridor, hoarse voice, swelling), a Breathing problem (wheeze, distress) or a Circulation problem (shock, collapse) and it is anaphylaxis. The answer is IM adrenaline into the thigh, dosed by age band, repeated after 5 minutes if needed.

blocks.text: Antihistamine is not a substitute for adrenaline. It is third line, after A, B and C problems are treated.

explain.body: Sudden onset, rapid progression, and Airway and/or Breathing and/or Circulation problems. Skin changes are common but absent in up to 20%.

test.q: Which finding, with sudden onset after an allergen, confirms an Airway problem?
test.why: A hoarse voice suggests airway swelling, an Airway problem.

whyNot.0: Urticaria is a skin change, not an A, B or C problem.
whyNot.2: Gastrointestinal symptoms alone do not define anaphylaxis.
whyNot.3: Itchy eyes are a mucosal symptom, not an airway problem.

explain.body: 1 mg/mL adrenaline IM, anterolateral thigh: over 12, 500 mcg (300 if small or prepubertal); 6 to 12, 300 mcg; 6 months to 6 years, 150 mcg; under 6 months, 100 to 150 mcg.

test.q: What volume of 1 mg/mL adrenaline gives 300 micrograms?

whyNot.1: 3 mL would be 3,000 micrograms, a ten-fold overdose.

explain.body: Repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if A, B or C problems persist and give a 10 mL/kg fluid bolus. After 2 IM doses without improvement: refractory; expert help for IV adrenaline infusion.

test.q: How soon can IM adrenaline be repeated if A, B or C problems persist?
test.why: RCUK: repeat IM adrenaline after 5 minutes if problems persist.

whyNot.1: 15 minutes is too long to wait with ongoing A, B or C problems.
whyNot.2: 30 minutes would leave the child untreated for too long.
whyNot.3: An hour is far beyond the 5-minute interval.

explain.body: Observe according to risk (2, 6 or 12 hours after resolution), refer every child to an allergy clinic, provide adrenaline auto-injectors with training and an emergency action plan.

test.q: Which is required before a child goes home after anaphylaxis?
test.why: RCUK (following NICE): all patients should be referred to a specialist allergy clinic, with an auto-injector, training and an action plan.

whyNot.0: Steroids are not routine after anaphylaxis.
whyNot.2: Routine daily antihistamines are not part of discharge advice.
whyNot.3: A chest X-ray is not part of routine discharge planning after anaphylaxis.
